narration: Welcome. This video is your viva preparation for the read-only page protection project in x86 x v 6. It has four parts. First, the problem and the background you need. Second, our solution and a walkthrough of every block of code we added. Third, the tests, the demo and the evidence. Fourth, the part your professor cares about most: how to change the code yourself. We will look at three example modifications, then go through the likely viva questions with short answers. One rule from your professor: AI help is allowed, but you must own every line. So pause the video often, and rewrite each function from memory.

slides.description: Viva preparation: read-only page protection in x86 xv6
bullets: Part 1: the problem and the background
Part 2: our solution, block by block
Part 3: tests, demo and evidence
Part 4: modify the code yourself, then viva questions
Rule: you must own and explain every line

narration: The assignment comes from the O S T E P virtual memory project. We must add two system calls to x v 6. m protect takes a page-aligned address and a length in pages, and makes those pages read-only. m unprotect does the reverse and restores write permission. Both return zero on success and minus one on an invalid request. A program must still be able to read a protected page. Only writes must be stopped. A write to a protected page must kill that process, not the whole system. Three extra requirements matter. A failed call must change nothing. The change must take effect immediately. And the permissions must survive fork, with parent and child independent afterwards. Null pointer protection, swapping and copy on write are out of scope.

slides.description: Read-only page protection in x86 xv6
bullets: `int mprotect(void *addr, int len)` makes `len` pages read-only
`int munprotect(void *addr, int len)` restores write access
`addr` is page-aligned and `len` counts pages, not bytes
Reads still work; a write must kill only that process
A failed call changes nothing; the change is immediate
Permissions survive `fork()` and stay independent

narration: Before the solution, the hardware. A page is 4096 bytes. A 32-bit virtual address splits into three fields. The top ten bits pick an entry in the page directory. The next ten bits pick an entry in a page table. The low twelve bits are the offset inside the page. The register C R 3 holds the physical address of the page directory. The entry that finally names the physical page is the page table entry, or P T E. Page number is the address divided by 4096. Offset is the address modulo 4096. A page-aligned address has offset zero. Alongside the physical page number, the P T E stores permission bits. Our whole project is about changing one of them.

bullets: Page size is 4096 bytes: offset = address % 4096
Top 10 bits: page directory index (`PDX`)
Next 10 bits: page table index (`PTX`)
`CR3` points to the page directory of the running process
The PTE holds the physical page plus permission bits

mermaidDiagram:
graph LR
  VA[Virtual address] --> PD[Page directory via CR3]
  PD -->|PDX| PT[Page table]
  PT -->|PTX| PTE[PTE: physical page + flags]
  PTE --> PA[Physical page + offset]

narration: This is mmu dot h. Here are the constants we use all project long. P G S I Z E is 4096. P G R O U N D D O W N rounds an address down to its page. P T E underscore P means present. P T E underscore W means writable. P T E underscore U means user accessible. P T E underscore A D D R keeps the physical page. P T E underscore F L A G S keeps the low twelve bits, the permissions. To clear a bit we AND with the inverse of the mask. To set a bit we OR with the mask. To test a bit we AND and compare with zero. Remember these three bit operations. The viva will probe them.

commentHints.comment: `PGSIZE` is 4096 bytes
`PGROUNDDOWN` clears the low 12 bits

`PTE_W`: writes are allowed. Our project toggles this bit
`PTE_U`: user mode may access the page
`PTE_ADDR` keeps the physical page
`PTE_FLAGS` keeps the low 12 permission bits

narration: Two hardware facts shape the design. First, the T L B. The processor caches translations together with their permissions. If we change a P T E, the processor may keep using the old cached copy. Writing C R 3 flushes this cache. That is why our code reloads C R 3. Second, look at entry dot S. It turns on paging and also sets C R 0 W P, the write-protect flag. With W P set, even the kernel obeys read-only pages. That sounds safe, but it creates a trap for us: if the kernel itself writes into a protected user page, it page faults in kernel mode. We will meet that again in part two.

commentHints.comment: `CR3` is loaded with the boot page directory
read control register 0
`CR0_PG` turns paging on; `CR0_WP` makes the kernel obey read-only pages

narration: This is the existing trap handler. When user code writes to a read-only page, the processor raises trap number fourteen, a page fault. The default case checks the saved code segment. If the fault came from user mode, x v 6 prints a message, marks the process killed, and exits it on the way back to user space. Decode the message. Error code seven is one plus two plus four. One means the page was present. Two means the access was a write. Four means user mode. So trap fourteen error seven is exactly: a user write to a present page without write permission. That is our protection firing. If the fault came from kernel mode, the branch above calls panic, and the whole machine stops.

commentHints.comment: kernel-mode fault: this is a kernel bug
`panic` stops the whole system
user mode: assume the process misbehaved
`err` and `rcr2()` give the reason and the faulting address
only this process is marked killed; the parent lives on

narration: Here is the whole solution on one slide. A user program calls m protect. A tiny assembly stub raises a software interrupt. The kernel dispatches to sys m protect, which fetches the two arguments and calls one shared helper, set u v m write. The helper validates the whole range first, then clears or sets only the writable bit, then reloads C R 3 to flush the T L B. The same helper serves m unprotect, so the two calls cannot drift apart. We then close a second door: system calls that write into user buffers must check the destination is writable, or the kernel itself would fault.

slides.description: Seven steps from C call to protected page
bullets: `mprotect()` stub raises `int $T_SYSCALL`
`sys_mprotect` fetches `addr` and `len`
`setuvmwrite()` validates the whole range first
Then it changes only `PTE_W` and reloads `CR3`
`read`, `fstat`, `pipe` now check their output buffers

graph TD
  U[User: mprotect addr len] --> S[usys.S stub: int T_SYSCALL]
  S --> D[syscall.c dispatch table]
  D --> P[sysproc.c: changeprotection]
  P --> H[vm.c: setuvmwrite]
  H --> V[Pass 1: validate every page]

narration: In sysproc dot c, change protection is the common front end. It fetches the first and second arguments with arg int. Remember arg int reads the word at stack pointer plus four plus four times n, skipping the return address. It then calls set u v m write with the current process's page directory, its size, the address, the length, and a flag: one for writable, zero for read-only. sys m protect passes zero. sys m unprotect passes one. One helper, two thin wrappers. Notice what is not here: no validation. The helper does all the checking, so the rules live in exactly one place.

narration: Now the heart of the project, set u v m write in vm dot c. It receives the page directory, the process size sz, the start address, the page count, and the desired state. The first check rejects an unaligned address, a count of zero or less, and a start at or beyond the process size. Because the count is a signed integer, negatives are caught here too. The second check is subtle. We do not compute address plus count times 4096 yet, because that product can overflow thirty-two bits. Instead we compare the count with how many whole pages fit between the start and the end of the process. Only after that is the end address safe to compute. Then pass one: for every page, walk the page table without allocating, and require the entry to exist, be present, and be a user page. The stack guard page has its user bit cleared, so it fails here.

commentHints.comment: returns 0 on success, -1 on an invalid request
aligned, positive, and starting inside the process
compare page COUNTS so nothing can overflow
now safe: this end is within `sz`
`walkpgdir(..., 0)` never allocates page tables
must be present and a user page; the guard page fails here

narration: Pass two runs only after pass one succeeded for every page, so it cannot fail halfway. That is how a bad page in the middle of a range never leaves a partial change. For each page we either OR in the writable bit, or AND with its inverse. All other bits, including the physical address, are untouched. Finally, lcr3 of V two P of the page directory reloads C R 3 and flushes this processor's T L B. We need V two P because C R 3 takes a physical address while the page directory pointer is a kernel virtual address. Without this line, the processor could keep using a cached writable translation, and the next write would wrongly succeed.

commentHints.comment: pass 1 loop ends: every page is valid
pass 2: only now do we modify anything
set the write bit
clear the write bit; other bits are unchanged
the TLB may cache the old permissions
reloading `CR3` flushes it; `V2P` makes the address physical

narration: Let us make the overflow concrete. Suppose the start address is 0x1000 and the count is 0x100000, which is two to the twentieth. Multiply the count by 4096, which is two to the twelfth, and you get two to the thirty-second. In thirty-two bit arithmetic that wraps around to zero. A naive check that computes start plus count times 4096 would see an end of 0x1000, which looks perfectly valid. Our check compares the count with the number of pages that actually fit, and correctly rejects it. If your professor asks why we wrote the check that way, this is the answer.

bullets: start = `0x1000`, count = `0x100000` (2^20 pages)
`count * 4096` is 2^32, which wraps to 0 in 32 bits
Naive end address = `0x1000`: looks valid, but is wrong
Ours: `count > (sz - va) / PGSIZE` is rejected correctly
Also catches negative counts and addresses that wrap

narration: Two design decisions deserve a clear answer. Why two passes? The specification says a failed call must leave previous permissions unchanged. If we changed pages while validating, a bad page late in the range would leave the earlier pages already modified. Validating everything first makes the update pass unable to fail. Why the T L B flush? Our own test proves it matters. A child first writes a page, so the processor caches a writable translation. It then calls m protect and writes again with no context switch. Only the C R 3 reload makes that second write fault. Earlier tests missed this, because a freshly forked child reloads C R 3 anyway. So we added a dedicated test.

bullets: Two passes make a failed call change nothing
Merging them left a program page read-only after a rejected range
`lcr3` flushes cached permissions so protection is immediate
A dedicated test fails if the flush is removed
Fork hid the bug in the first version of the tests

narration: Fork needed no change. Look at the existing copy u v m. For every page of the parent, it reads the flags with P T E underscore F L A G S, allocates a fresh physical page, copies the contents, and maps the child's copy with the same flags. So if the parent page is read-only, the child's copy is read-only too. That is inheritance. The two copies are different physical pages with different P T Es. Later changes by one process cannot affect the other. Our tests check both directions: a child unprotecting its copy leaves the parent protected, and a child protecting its copy leaves the parent writable.

commentHints.comment: builds the child's page table
find the parent's PTE; never allocates
physical page of the parent
all permission bits are remembered, including `PTE_W`
the child gets its own physical page
contents are copied
mapped with the SAME flags, so read-only is inherited

narration: Now the problem we found by testing. A user write to a protected page faults in user mode, and the process dies. But what if the kernel writes into a protected user page for the user? The read system call copies data into a user buffer from inside the kernel. Because C R 0 W P is set, a kernel write to a read-only page faults in kernel mode. The trap handler treats any kernel fault as a kernel bug and calls panic. We reproduced this: read from a pipe into a protected page crashed the guest with panic trap, before the fix. The rule we adopted: if the kernel will write into a user buffer, check that every page of it is writable first, and return minus one if not. If the kernel only reads the buffer, as write does, a protected page is fine.

bullets: `read()` into a protected page: kernel-mode write fault
`trap()` treats kernel-mode faults as bugs: `panic: trap`
Fix: check output buffers are writable, return `-1` if not
`write()` only READS the buffer, so protected sources are fine
`copyout()` also honours `PTE_W`

narration: The new function check u v m write takes a page directory, a start address, and a length. A length of zero is fine, nothing will be written. Otherwise it computes the last byte's page, and loops from the first page to the last, so buffers that span several pages are covered, including a writable page followed by a protected one. For each page, all three bits must be set: present, user, and writable. The expression masks the entry with the three flags and compares with all three. Anything less returns minus one. Like pass one of our main helper, it never allocates, so checking cannot change the page tables.

Otherwise it calls check u v m write for the same range, so the buffer must also be writable. Using one new function keeps the three callers identical. The size argument is the buffer length that the system call will write.

narration: Three system calls write into user memory, and each changed by exactly one word: arg ptr became arg ptr w. In sys read, the destination buffer p is checked before file read copies data into it. In sys fstat, the struct stat that will be filled is checked. In sys pipe, the two-integer array that receives the file descriptors is checked. Notice what did not change: sys write still uses plain arg ptr, because it only reads the user buffer. Our test confirms that writing from a protected page prints the data.

narration: One more door. Copy out writes through the kernel's own mapping of the physical page, which is always writable. It would silently bypass a read-only user mapping. So after finding the kernel address, we also call check u v m write for that one page, and fail if it is not writable. In today's x v 6 the only caller is exec, which writes to a brand-new stack, so behaviour does not change. But the protection guarantee is now complete.

narration: Part three: proving it works. In vmtest dot c, allocate pages uses sbrk to round the heap up to a page boundary and return fresh pages, so a test never protects the stack or malloc data. The key helper is child write faults. x v 6's wait returns no exit status, so we use a pipe as a marker. The child writes to the address, and only if that succeeds, writes one byte to the pipe. The parent reads the pipe. End of file means the child died before the marker, so the write faulted. A byte means the write went through. That is how a test distinguishes a blocked write from a successful one.

`sbrk` grows the heap by the padding plus the pages
returns 1 if the child was stopped by a fault
a child, so the fault kills it and not the test
the write under test
marker: only reached if the write succeeded
EOF means the child died before the marker
count it; the runner checks this number later

Unprotect, write a new value, read it back. And a child writing now succeeds. Each line is a check, and every check prints ok or FAIL, with a description, so a failure tells you exactly which behaviour broke.

narration: This is the test I would highlight in a viva. The child writes the page first, which loads a writable translation into the T L B. Then it calls m protect and writes again immediately, with no context switch. If m protect forgot to reload C R 3, the cached writable translation would let the second write succeed, and the marker byte would reach the parent. With the reload, the second write faults. We checked this by deleting the reload line: the test failed with the message m protect takes effect immediately. Then we restored the line.

Why walk page directory with allocate zero? Validation must not create page tables, and a bad address must not allocate memory. What happens without the C R 3 reload? The processor may keep a cached writable translation, so a write could still succeed. Why V two P? C R 3 holds a physical address.

narration: Why did read into a protected buffer panic the kernel? C R 0 W P makes kernel writes obey read-only pages, and a kernel-mode fault calls panic. How is it fixed? The output buffers of read, fstat and pipe are checked first, and the call returns minus one. Why is write from a protected buffer still allowed? The kernel only reads it. What happens to protected pages after exec, or after sbrk shrinks the heap? Exec builds a fresh address space. Shrinking frees the pages normally. New pages are writable. Is the check-then-write safe on a multi-processor kernel with threads? No, you would need locking or fault handling. On one processor with no threads, nothing can change the page between check and write. Why use a pipe in the tests? Because wait returns no exit status in x v 6.
